topics.explanation: Calling a model is the easy part; in production you own what happens around it — speed, cost, capacity and reliability — and each idea in the session maps to a decision you will be asked to make.
revision_points: Each idea today maps to a decision you will be asked to make.

source_reference.quote: In production you own what happens around it: speed, cost, capacity and reliability

topics.explanation: The one-line refresher of the five Day 1 words defines latency as how fast one request starts and throughput as how many are served at once.

source_reference.quote: Latency is how fast one request starts; throughput is how many we serve at once.

topics.explanation: Named as one of four ideas that decide real-world speed: batching processes requests together.

source_reference.quote: batching (process requests together)

topics.explanation: Named as one of four ideas that decide real-world speed: concurrency is many requests in flight at once.

source_reference.quote: concurrency (many in flight at once)

topics.explanation: Named as one of four ideas that decide real-world speed: queueing is waiting for a free slot.

source_reference.quote: queueing (waiting for a free slot)

topics.explanation: Named as one of four ideas that decide real-world speed: a cold start is the delay before a sleeping model can answer.

source_reference.quote: cold starts (the delay before a sleeping model can answer)

topics.explanation: Every request passes the same six stages: it arrives, may wait in a queue, has its prompt processed (prefill), generates tokens one by one (decode), shares the GPU with others (batching), and streams back.

source_reference.quote: Every request passes the same six stages

topics.explanation: The tokenizer from Day 1 cuts your text into tokens and the request is handed to the server; from then on everything the model sees is a sequence of token IDs, not words.

source_reference.quote: everything the model sees is a sequence of token IDs, not words

topics.explanation: The server may not start your request immediately; if every slot is busy it waits in a queue, and that waiting time is part of TTFT and under heavy load often dominates it.

source_reference.quote: That waiting time is part of TTFT

topics.explanation: Prefill: the model reads the entire prompt in one pass, builds its internal state, then emits the first token; a longer prompt means more work before that first token, so a higher TTFT.

source_reference.quote: the model reads the entire prompt in one pass, builds its internal state, then emits the first token

topics.explanation: Decode: each new token depends on the tokens before it, so the model produces them one at a time; the gap between two consecutive tokens is TPOT and sets how fast text streams.

source_reference.quote: The gap between two consecutive tokens is TPOT, and it sets how fast text streams.

topics.explanation: To keep an expensive GPU busy, providers batch many requests together: more requests are served per second (throughput), but your own request may have to wait for the batch (latency).

source_reference.quote: More requests are served per second (throughput), but your own request may have to wait for the batch (latency).

topics.explanation: TTFT = queueing + prefill. TPOT = decode time per token. Total latency is everything combined, roughly TTFT + (output tokens - 1) x TPOT.
revision_points: This is the one diagram to remember from today.
Remember: TTFT = queueing + prefill, TPOT = decode.

source_reference.quote: TTFT = queueing + prefill. TPOT = decode time per token.

topics.explanation: Aention needs the keys (K) and values (V) of every earlier token; without a cache the model recomputes them for the whole sequence at every step, while with a KV cache each token’s K and V are computed once, stored and reused.

source_reference.quote: each token’s K and V are computed once, stored and reused

topics.explanation: The cache stores K and V for every token, in every layer, for every request in the batch — about 0.8 MB per token for a 13B model — and it competes with the weights for GPU memory and sets how many requests fit at once.

source_reference.quote: about 0.8 MB per token for a 13B model

topics.explanation: Static batching waits for the slowest request before starting anything new, so finished slots sit idle; continuous (iteration-level) batching refills a freed slot at the very next step, so the GPU stays full and newcomers wait less.

source_reference.quote: Continuous (iteration-level) batching refills a freed slot at the very next step

topics.explanation: Each step the scheduler decides who joins the batch; a long prompt can hog a step and stall everyone’s decoding, so engines slice it, and when KV memory runs out they pause requests or turn them away.

source_reference.quote: When KV memory runs out they pause requests or turn them away.

topics.explanation: Larger models are usually stronger but slower and pricier per token; smaller models are cheaper and snappier but weaker on complex tasks.
revision_points: Latency, cost and quality move together.

source_reference.quote: Larger models are usually stronger but slower and pricier per token

topics.explanation: Picking a model is a trade-off, not a ranking: the slide’s questions are how long this task can wait, and how wrong it can be. There is no universal answer.

source_reference.quote: There is no universal answer.

topics.explanation: Instead of one model for everything, a router picks the model per request: easy ones go to a small, fast model, hard ones to a large, careful one. The slide calls this a soft preview of Day 10.

source_reference.quote: a router picks the model per request

topics.explanation: Average latency hides most of these problems; teams watch a small dashboard of percentiles for TTFT and TPOT, token counts, queue and cache health, and output quality. Day 10 (observability) goes deeper.

source_reference.quote: percentiles for TTFT and TPOT, token counts, queue and cache health, and output quality

topics.explanation: In production nobody tells you 'the KV cache is full' — you get symptoms; knowing the concepts turns a vague complaint into a short list of suspects, and each suspect lives in one stage of the pipeline.

source_reference.quote: each suspect lives in one stage of the pipeline

topics.explanation: In GPT-2/3’s tokenizer, usernames from Reddit’s r/counting forum such as ' SolidGoldMagikarp' became single tokens, yet barely appeared in the model’s training data; asked about them the models denied, hallucinated or produced gibberish. Cited by the source to LessWrong (Feb 2023) and follow-ups by the researchers.

source_reference.quote: became single tokens, yet barely appeared in the model’s training data

topics.explanation: GPT-4o launched in May 2024 with a new 200k-token tokenizer; researchers found that most of its longest Chinese tokens were spam, gambling and adult-site phrases, because the corpus the tokenizer learned from had been polluted by hijacked web pages. Cited by the source to MIT Technology Review (May 2024).

source_reference.quote: the corpus the tokenizer learned from had been polluted by hijacked web pages

topics.explanation: Anthropic’s 2025 postmortem: a routing bug sent short-context requests to servers set up for the 1M-token context window; at the worst hour 16% of Sonnet 4 requests were aected, and sticky routing kept some users on the wrong servers. Cited by the source to Anthropic Engineering, "A postmortem of three recent issues" (Sept 17, 2025).

source_reference.quote: a routing bug sent short-context requests to servers set up for the 1M-token context window

topics.explanation: Berkeley’s vLLM team found that 2023 serving systems wasted 60-80% of KV-cache memory on fragmentation and over-reservation, which capped batch sizes; paging the cache (PagedAention) cut waste below 4% and raised throughput 2-4x. Cited by the source to the vLLM team (June 2023).

source_reference.quote: cut waste below 4% and raised throughput 2-4x
